orient: Narrator: Nelly Dean, still telling her story to Lockwood. It is the summer of 1797, a few weeks after Edgar left Thrushcross Grange to visit his dying sister, and thirteen-year-old Cathy is waiting at home with Nelly for news.

notes.n: Letters announcing a death were written on paper with a black border.

notes.g: Isabella, Edgar's sister, who fled from her husband Heathcliff in Chapter XVII.
Buy black mourning clothes for Cathy.
notes.n: Families wore black for weeks or months after a relative's death.

notes.g: Isabella's son, Linton, now about twelve.
notes.n: 'Linton' is the boy's first name: Isabella named him after her own family. His father is Heathcliff.

notes.g: Here 'Catherine' is Edgar's daughter, Cathy, not her dead mother.

notes.m: 'Sanguine' means optimistic. Nothing to do with blood, though the word comes from the Latin for blood.

notes.n: Unlike Hareton, whom she refused to accept as a cousin in Chapter XVIII.

notes.t: attired in her new black frock
notes.g: Dressed in her new black mourning dress.

notes.t: impressed her with no definite sorrow

notes.m: Not 'did me a favour'. 'Oblige' here means compel.

notes.t: Linton is just six months younger than I am
notes.g: Linton, her cousin, is six months younger than Cathy.
notes.n: Careful: 'Linton' now means two people. Edgar is usually 'Mr. Linton', 'Edgar Linton', 'my master' or 'uncle'. Plain 'Linton' usually means the boy, but not always: check each time.

notes.t: the swells and hollows of mossy turf
notes.g: The rises and dips of mossy grass.

notes.t: a beautiful lock of his hair
notes.g: A cut curl of his hair.
notes.n: Locks of hair were common keepsakes, often kept in lockets or little boxes.
Flax fibre, used to make linen, is a pale yellowish grey.

notes.g: The coach used for long journeys.

notes.t: a sickly peevishness in his aspect
notes.g: A sickly, whiny look about him.
Edgar, the second person just mentioned, saw me looking.

notes.m: 'Directly' meant immediately, not 'in a straight line'.

notes.g: Be careful not to upset her.

notes.m: A 'salute' was a kiss or greeting, not a military salute.

notes.t: put on as sad a countenance

notes.g: Where the tea things were set out.
Edgar's patience had been badly tested.
The whiny, sickly boy in his care.

notes.t: make a pet of her little cousin
notes.g: Fuss over her cousin like a pet.

notes.t: offering him tea in her saucer
notes.g: Giving him tea from her saucer.
notes.n: People often poured hot tea into the saucer to cool it. Cathy feeds him like a baby.

notes.t: what playmates and instructors they’ll be
notes.g: What fine companions and teachers they'll make (said ironically).

notes.t: would not suffer me to leave him
notes.m: 'Suffer' here means allow, not feel pain.

notes.g: A candle in a holder, carried to light the way up to bed.

notes.n: Servants who had known him from boyhood might still call him 'Mr. Edgar'.

notes.g: Dressed in his best Sunday clothes.

notes.t: It’s Maister Linton I mun spake to
notes.g: It's Mr. Linton I must speak to.
Waving me out of the way with contempt.
Give me your message to pass on.
Determined not to let me act as go-between.
The visitor who had come at such a bad time.

notes.s: Hathecliff has sent me for his lad
notes.tr: Heathcliff has sent me for his boy, and I mustn't go back without him.

notes.t: her commendations of him to his care
notes.g: Her requests that Edgar look after him.

notes.t: nothing left but to resign him
notes.g: Nothing to do but give him up.
In my care as his guardian.
notes.n: In law a father's claim was much stronger: a father then had almost total rights over his children.

notes.tr: No! That means nothing. Heathcliff takes no notice of the mother, or of you either; but he'll have his boy, and I must take him. So now you know!

notes.g: Takes no account of; doesn't care about.

notes.t: aiding the indignant elder with a lift by the arm
notes.g: Helping the angry old man out by the arm.
notes.n: A polite way of saying Edgar pushed Joseph out.

notes.tr: Very well! Tomorrow he'll come himself, and you throw him out if you dare!
